opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic story is something like this. GPT-4 could already do chain-of-thought reasoning in some sense: if you prompted it to think step by step, it would write out intermediate steps, and that helped somewhat. But that reasoning was mostly imitative. It had learned to produce text that looks like reasoning from human-written data, and it wasn't especially good at using that reasoning to actually get the right answer. It would often go down a wrong path and not notice, or produce something superficially plausible that didn't hold together.

What changed with o1 and then o3, as I understand it, is that these models were trained with a lot of reinforcement learning on tasks where you can check the answer: math problems, programming problems, things with verifiable outcomes. The model generates a long chain of thought, you see whether it got the answer right, and you reinforce the reasoning that led to correct answers. Over a lot of training, the model learns reasoning strategies that actually work, rather than ones that just look like what a human would write. You see behaviors like backtracking, noticing its own mistakes, trying an alternative approach, checking its work. Those emerge, or get strengthened, because they're useful for getting the right answer.

So I'd describe it as going from chain of thought as a kind of prompting trick to chain of thought as a capability the model has been directly optimized for. And that's a pretty big deal, because it means you can convert more inference-time compute into better performance in a way you mostly couldn't before. If the model thinks longer, it does meaningfully better on hard problems.

The gains were really large on the domains where this training applies. On competition math and competitive programming, the jump from GPT-4 to o3 was enormous, much bigger than you'd have predicted from just extrapolating the pretraining scaling trend. It's less clear how much it transfers to fuzzier domains where it's harder to verify the answer, and I think that's one of the key open questions. Some of it seems to transfer, models seem somewhat better at careful reasoning in general, but the most dramatic improvements are concentrated where you have good feedback signals.

From an AI safety perspective, I have somewhat mixed feelings. On one hand, it's nice that a lot of the cognition is now happening in natural language that we can read, which gives us a potential window into what the model is doing. On the other hand, it's not obvious that window will stay faithful as you apply more optimization pressure, and RL on outcomes is the kind of training that could produce models that pursue goals in ways we didn't intend. So it's a capabilities advance that I think really matters for timelines, and it also changes the shape of the safety problem in ways we're still figuring out.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-4 would often go down a wrong path and not notice, identifying difficulty catching and recovering from mistakes.

r002.rationale: It says GPT-4 could already perform chain-of-thought reasoning when prompted, then describes o1 and o3 training as strengthening reasoning that works.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing to understand is that GPT-4 could already do chain-of-thought reasoning in some sense — you could prompt it to think step by step and it would get better results on math problems and so on. But the chain of thought it produced was basically an imitation of how humans write out reasoning. It was trained to predict text, and then a bit of RLHF on top, and so when it reasoned it was sort of doing a plausible impression of a person working through a problem. It wasn't actually optimized for the reasoning to be useful.

What changed with o1 and o3 is that OpenAI did reinforcement learning directly on the reasoning process, where the reward is based on whether you get the right answer at the end. So the model is now being trained to produce chains of thought that actually cause it to get the correct answer, rather than ones that look like what a human would write. And once you do that, the model learns a bunch of things that are pretty natural: it learns to check its work, to backtrack when it notices something is off, to try a different approach when the first one isn't panning out, to spend more tokens on harder problems. These are all things GPT-4 basically didn't do unless you hand-held it a lot, and even then it was shaky.

I think the right mental model is that pretraining gives you a model with a lot of latent capability — it knows a huge amount, it can do many individual reasoning steps — but it's not very good at stringing those steps together reliably over a long horizon. The RL is teaching it how to actually use that capability in an extended way. And a key thing is that this works because, for domains like math and coding, you have verifiable answers, so you can just check and get a clean reward signal. That's why we've seen the biggest gains in those areas and comparatively less in, say, creative writing or open-ended philosophy.

The other piece is that this unlocks scaling along a new axis. Before, if you wanted a better model, you basically had to do a bigger pretraining run. Now you can scale the RL — do more of it, on more problems — and you can also scale inference-time compute, just let the model think for longer. o3 is a pretty striking demonstration of the latter: on something like ARC-AGI or the hard math benchmarks, letting it think for a very long time gets you results that would have seemed quite far off a year earlier.

I will say I think people sometimes overstate how qualitatively different this is. In some sense it's "just" RL on top of the same kind of model, and a lot of the capabilities were latently there. But the practical effect is pretty large, and I think it's clearly made the near-term trajectory of AI faster than I would have guessed a couple years ago. It also has implications for safety that I think are kind of mixed — on the one hand the reasoning is written out in natural language and we can read it, which is great for oversight; on the other hand, the more you optimize the chain of thought for outcomes rather than for being a faithful human-readable trace, the more pressure there is for it to drift away from something we can actually interpret.

r001.rationale: The response says o1/o3 learned to backtrack when something is off, while GPT-4 generally did not do this without substantial hand-holding.

r002.rationale: It says GPT-4 could already reason step by step and describes RL as teaching the model to use latent capabilities more reliably, framing the change as refinement of an existing ability.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things to distinguish. One is whether a model can produce useful intermediate reasoning at all. GPT-4 could already do that: if you asked it to work through a problem step by step, that would often improve its answer. But it wasn’t necessarily very good at deciding what to spend that reasoning on, noticing when an approach had failed, or trying a different approach.

The other thing is training the model to use that reasoning effectively. You can train on problems where you can check the final answer, let the model generate a long chain of thought, and reinforce the trajectories that get the answer right. That gives you a way to improve the reasoning without having to specify exactly what every intermediate step should look like.

My understanding is that this is a substantial part of the transition to models like o1 and o3, though I don’t know the precise training recipe. It’s not just taking GPT-4 and telling it to think for longer. You’re training a model that can make better use of the extra computation.

And then you get this additional axis of scaling: how much computation you spend answering a particular question. That’s particularly useful for tasks where there’s a lot of productive work you can do before answering, like checking a mathematical argument or trying different ways to solve a coding problem. It doesn’t mean that thinking longer will reliably fix every mistake. But it makes the amount of computation available at inference time a much more important part of the picture.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-4 was not necessarily good at noticing when an approach had failed or trying another approach, identifying difficulty recovering from mistakes.

r002.rationale: It says GPT-4 already could produce useful intermediate reasoning and frames o1/o3’s gains as training that capability to be used more effectively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two things worth separating. One is how much useful reasoning a model can do in a single forward pass, and the other is how effectively it can use a large number of tokens to work through a problem.

GPT-4 could already benefit from writing out its reasoning. But if it made a mistake, it often wouldn’t notice, or it would continue down an unproductive path. With models like o1 and o3, training specifically rewards getting the answer right after doing a substantial amount of reasoning. That can teach the model to check its work, try another approach, and spend more effort on the parts of a problem where that effort is useful.

So I wouldn’t necessarily interpret the improvement as each individual step becoming vastly more sophisticated. Part of it is getting much better at composing lots of steps into a successful overall process. And that matters because it gives you another way to improve performance: you can spend more computation at inference time.

There are limits to that. If the model doesn’t have the relevant concepts, thinking for longer might not help. And a long, plausible-looking chain of thought isn’t necessarily correct. But these models seem substantially better at turning additional reasoning time into better answers, especially on problems where the answer can be checked.

r001.rationale: It says GPT-4 often failed to notice a mistake or continued down an unproductive path.

r002.rationale: It says GPT-4 could already benefit from writing out reasoning, and frames o1/o3’s gains as better composing steps into a successful process rather than vastly more sophisticated individual steps.
